originalTitle: The words in the README, before lesson 0

blocks.text: This section exists because the README (and the lessons that follow) assume you already know what a "pass", "IR", and "CFG" are. It is not part of the numbered lessons; read it once, then start at lesson 1.
What is a compiler, and where does LLVM fit?

A compiler translates a program you wrote in a language like C++ into machine instructions a CPU executes. Modern compilers are built in stages, and each stage reads one representation of the program, inspects or improves it, and hands a new representation to the next stage:

C++ source  ->  [front end]  ->  LLVM IR  ->  [mid-end: passes]  ->  LLVM IR'
            ->  [back end]  ->  machine code  ->  object file  ->  executable

**Clang** is the front end: it turns `.c`/`.cpp` files into LLVM IR. **LLVM** is the rest of the pipeline's infrastructure: the intermediate representation itself, plus libraries of analyses (things that inspect the IR and report facts about it) and transformations (things that rewrite it), and the tools to load and run them.
MiniShield does not compile C++ programs. It is a plugin loaded into `opt`, LLVM's command-line IR tool (below), which then runs MiniShield's passes over `.ll` IR files.
What is LLVM IR?

LLVM IR (intermediate representation) describes a program in terms of typed values and instructions, before any specific CPU is chosen. A minimal example (this is the entire `minishield-input.ll` fixture):

items: `@add_one` is a **function**; `i32` is a 32-bit integer type; `%x` is a typed value.

`entry:` names a **basic block**: a straight-line run of instructions with a single entry point and no jumps inside it. A block always ends with a **terminator** instruction that transfers control (`ret`, `br`, ...).

`%result = add i32 %x, 1` is one **instruction**; the name `%result` is defined exactly once and only used after that definition. This "define once, use later" property is called **SSA** (static single assignment).
The files in `tests/ir/` (for example `tests/ir/phi.ll`) are handwritten text IR, one small function each.

blocks.text: What is a pass?

A **pass** is one program-level inspection or transformation that LLVM runs over the IR. A pass receives an object (here: a `Function`), inspects or changes it, and returns a result describing what it did. Think of a pass as a function that LLVM calls for you, once per function, in the order you scheduled.

MiniShield has two so far: `StatsPass` only counts instructions and prints a report (a read-only pass), and `FlatteningPass`, which will restructure the function's control flow (a transformation pass, not yet implemented).
What is `opt`, and what is a pass plugin?
`opt` is LLVM's command-line tool for IR: it reads an IR file, runs a **pipeline** of passes, and writes IR back (or just prints diagnostics). Out of the box, `opt` only knows LLVM's built-in passes.

A **pass plugin** is a small shared library (here `build/libMiniShield.so`) that `opt` loads at start-up when you pass `-load-pass-plugin=...`. The loading happens through the system's `dlopen()` mechanism: the library is read into memory and its exported entry point `llvmGetPassPluginInfo` is called. That entry point hands back the pass names the plugin provides (`minishield-stats`, `minishield-flatten`), so after loading, `-passes='function(minishield-stats)'` can name your pass. The plugin is therefore a load-time relationship with `opt`, not a link-time one (lesson 2 explains why that decides the CMake library type).
The comma in `-passes='function(minishield-stats),verify'` is the pipeline: run the named function pass on every function, then run the built-in `verify` pass over the module.
What are control flow, a CFG, and control-flow flattening?

**Control flow** is the order in which a program's instructions execute, determined by its branches. An `if` statement means "these instructions, or those, depending on a condition", and a `while` loop means "these instructions, possibly again".
The **control-flow graph (CFG)** makes that order explicit: basic blocks are nodes, and every possible "go to next block" transfer is an edge. The function in `tests/ir/phi.ll` has four blocks:

entry -> left  -> join
       \       /
        right ->   (join ends the function with ret)
`entry` has two successors (its conditional branch can choose either), `join` has none (it ends in `ret`).

**Control-flow flattening** is a transformation that takes a structured CFG like that and rewires it into a shallower, harder-to-follow shape: many small basic blocks, all at the same level, joined by a dispatcher — usually a loop plus a big `switch` over block identifiers that decides which block runs next. The program still computes the same results, but the visible control flow becomes one long sequential loop instead of the original if/else or loop structure. Flattening is used in binary hardening and obfuscation (attackers' tools find it harder to reconstruct the original logic), which is why MiniShield's goal is a safe flattener: it must accept only functions whose flow it fully understands and leave everything else byte-for-byte untouched.

**Natural loops** (mentioned in the README and lesson 17) are the loops a specific standard algorithm finds: take a **back edge** (an edge from a block to an earlier block that dominates it — dominates meaning every path from the entry to that block passes through it) and collect every block that can reach the loop header without going through the exit. LLVM's `LoopAnalysis` computes exactly these; in `tests/ir/loop.ll` the edge `body -> header` is the single back edge, and the natural loop is `{header, body}`.
What do "function eligibility" and "diagnostic stub" mean?

**Eligibility** is the yes/no decision made before a flattening pass rewrites a function: is this function's shape one the pass can handle? The current policy (lesson 23) rejects, among other things, functions with exception handling, coroutine intrinsics, block addresses used as values, or terminators the pass does not model (only `br`, `switch`, `ret`, `unreachable` are accepted). An accepted function is **eligible**; a rejected one must be left completely unchanged — lesson 25 shows how to prove that with a diff. Eligibility is a conservative "we can handle this shape" decision, not a proof that flattening is safe in general.

A **stub** is a placeholder implementation: the interface exists and runs, but the real work is not there yet. At the start of this project, `FlatteningPass::run` only prints the function name and block count; it changes nothing. The word **diagnostic** (as in "diagnostic stub") says the stub's job is to report observations, not to transform. By lesson 23 the stub also prints the eligibility decision.
What are conda, CMake, and Ninja, in one line each?

items: **Conda** (here via **Miniforge**, a conda distribution that defaults to the conda-forge channel) is a package and environment manager. The `minishield` environment is a self-contained directory with its own compiler, LLVM 23.1.5, build tools, and libraries, so the project does not depend on what the host machine happens to have installed. "Activating" it puts that environment's tools at the front of the shell's command search path.
**CMake** is the configure step: it reads `CMakeLists.txt`, locates the installed LLVM, and generates build instructions. It does not compile anything itself.
**Ninja** is the build step: it executes the generated instructions (`build/build.ninja`), compiling only the changed files and linking the plugin.

blocks.text: The four-step chain — create the environment, activate it, configure with CMake, build with Ninja — is exactly the lesson 1 checkpoint.
What do the `opt` flags in the README mean?

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-stats),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-output.ll

items: `-load-pass-plugin=...` loads MiniShield's `.so` so its pass names exist.
`-passes=...` is the pipeline to run; `function(X)` means "run X once per function in the module".
`verify` is a built-in pass that checks the IR's structural rules.
`-S` prints the result as text IR; without it, `opt` writes compact binary IR by default.
`-o file` writes the transformed IR to a file; `-disable-output` keeps the IR in memory and writes nothing — used when you only want the diagnostics the pass printed.

blocks.text: What is a fixture?

A **fixture** is a small, stable input file kept in the repository (here the `.ll` files under `tests/ir/`) whose expected results are known by hand. You run your tool on the fixture and compare the output to the expectation (the table in lesson 12). "Fixture" comes from test setup being fixed in place: nobody edits a fixture to make a test pass.
Valid vs. correct: what `verify` does and does not prove

`verify` checks that the IR obeys LLVM's structural rules: types agree, every value is defined exactly once before use (SSA), every PHI node has an incoming value from each predecessor block, return types match the function's type, and so on. IR that passes is **valid** (well-formed).

**Correctness** — does the transformed program compute the same results, with the same side effects, as the input — is a separate, stronger property. `verify` does not check it: a pass can emit perfectly valid IR that behaves differently. That is why lesson 14's empty-diff check (the pass must leave the IR unchanged while it is a stub) and, later, real testing, are the actual safety nets.

originalTitle: Create the minishield Conda environment

blocks.text: Day 1 builds toward one decision — which functions a control-flow-flattening pass may touch. Everything before that decision is inspection, and inspection needs a plugin that actually loads. This part is the ground every later lesson stands on: a consistent Conda toolchain and a CMake project that turns your source into a loadable library.
Goal: give the project one consistent Linux C++ toolchain, LLVM release, build system, and test library.
The recorded environment was originally created with this command (confirmed in its conda-meta/history):
conda create -y -n minishield -c conda-forge clang lld llvmdev gtest cmake ninja

Conda downloaded prebuilt packages and their dependencies. It did not compile LLVM from source. That unpinned command resolved LLVM/Clang 23.1.5 in this study session; running it later can select a different release.
Create the study environment reproducibly
For a fresh setup on Linux x86-64, first install Conda or Miniforge and initialize its Bash integration if necessary. Then, from this repository:

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate minishield

The environment name comes from name: minishield in environment.yml. Creating the environment installs packages into a separate prefix; activating it changes the current shell's PATH and sets CONDA_PREFIX so commands resolve to this toolchain. Activation does not compile this project.
If Conda is installed but activation is unavailable in Bash, load the shell hook from your own installation. In the recorded machine it was:

source "$HOME/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh"
conda activate minishield

The setup file pins clang, lld, and llvmdev to 23.1.5 to keep the plugin's headers and runtime compatible. It is a study environment specification, not a byte-for-byte lockfile of every dependency. Package availability and platform still matter.
Know what each dependency does

rows: C/C++ compiler for the plugin and future input programs
LLVM headers, library development files, and CMake package metadata
LLVM linker available for toolchain work
GoogleTest for the later C++ test suite
Configures the project and generates Ninja build instructions
Executes the generated compile and link rules
Standard C++ headers such as type_traits, matching this session's runtime

blocks.text: The initial environment had the C++ runtime but lacked its development headers. During the build lesson we added libstdcxx-devel_linux-64 16.2.0. The repository specification includes it from the start. A missing type_traits error concerns C++ standard-library headers, not the path to LLVM headers.
For an existing environment missing those headers, the normal package-install command is:
conda install -n minishield -c conda-forge libstdcxx-devel_linux-64=16.2.0
Verify the environment before building

conda activate minishield
clang --version
clang++-23 --version
opt --version
llvm-config --version
cmake --version
ninja --version
The LLVM tools should report the same 23.1.5 release. This environment exposes clang++-23 rather than a plain clang++; pin that compiler in CMake instead of falling back to the host compiler.
Before linking in this environment:
export LIBRARY_PATH="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib"

LIBRARY_PATH supplies link-time library search paths used by the compiler driver. It is different from LLVM_DIR, which tells CMake where to find LLVMConfig.cmake, and from LD_LIBRARY_PATH, which affects runtime library loading.
Checkpoint: distinguish these four operations: install the environment, activate the environment, configure the project with CMake, and build the project with Ninja. They are separate steps.

originalTitle: Understand what CMake is configuring

blocks.text: Task: read CMakeLists.txt and identify the target named MiniShield.

add_library(MiniShield MODULE ...) describes a loadable plugin. The listed .cpp files are compiled and linked into build/libMiniShield.so. The MODULE library is loaded by opt at runtime through -load-pass-plugin.
A hello-world CMakeLists to start from
The smallest CMakeLists.txt that does anything useful is three lines:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.15)
project(HelloWorld CXX)
add_executable(hello main.cpp)

items: `cmake_minimum_required` sets a version floor: CMake refuses to run if it is older than this.
`project(HelloWorld CXX)` names the project and enables the C++ compiler.
`add_executable` defines one target: a program. CMake compiles `main.cpp` and links `build/hello`.

blocks.text: With that file, `cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build` works and you run `./build/hello`. Notice what is not there: no package discovery, no compiler flags, no include paths, no link libraries, no output location. Every one of those omissions is possible because hello-world has no dependencies and produces a program that you run directly.

MiniShield's CMakeLists.txt has none of that by accident: every extra line exists because the project consumes a prebuilt third-party library and produces a plugin that `opt` loads, not a program you run.
MiniShield's CMakeLists, line by line
The project's file makes four moves.
**Move 1 — pick the language and standard (lines 1–6).**

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.15)
project(MiniShield CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)

Same opening as hello-world, plus decisions hello-world can skip: LLVM 23's headers require C++20, so the standard is pinned (`REQUIRED ON` makes a downgrade an error, not a warning), and `CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS` writes `build/compile_commands.json` so clangd and IDEs can index the project.
**Move 2 — find LLVM (lines 10–12).**

set(LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB ON)
find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)
message(STATUS "Found llvm ${LLVM_PACKAGE_VERSION} at ${LLVM_DIR}")

Hello-world needs no packages; this project needs the prebuilt LLVM the Conda environment installed. `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)` locates the `LLVMConfig.cmake` that the configure step's `-DLLVM_DIR` points at; that file defines `LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS`, `LLVM_DEFINITIONS`, and the imported `LLVM` target this file uses in the next moves. `REQUIRED` makes a missing LLVM a hard configure error instead of a later, mysterious failure.
**Move 3 — define the target (lines 16–19).**

add_library(MiniShield MODULE
    lib/Plugin.cpp
    lib/FlatteningPass.cpp)

This is the hello-world divergence in one keyword. Hello-world says `add_executable`: build a program with a `main()`. MiniShield says `add_library ... MODULE`: build a loadable shared library with no `main()`. Nothing links against MiniShield; `opt` `dlopen()`s it at run time. (`STATIC` would be an archive no one can `dlopen`; `SHARED` would declare a "you may link me" relationship that does not exist — see the `add_library` deep dive below.)
**Move 4 — attach the requirements (lines 21–32).**

separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})
target_compile_definitions(MiniShield PRIVATE ${MS_LLVM_DEFS})
target_include_directories(MiniShield PRIVATE
    ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS}
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)
set_target_properties(MiniShield PROPERTIES LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR})

Hello-world compiles against the standard library and needs none of this.
The plugin has five requirements, all target-scoped and all `PRIVATE`
because nothing links against MiniShield. Each command answers one
question; they configure the target, and compilation and linking happen
later, when the build runs.

**`separate_arguments` — turn a flag string into a list.** CMake has no
array type: a "list" is a `;`-separated string. `LLVMConfig.cmake` stores
`LLVM_DEFINITIONS` as *one* space-joined string (e.g.
`"-D_GNU_SOURCE -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -D__STDC_FORMAT_MACROS"`), so
passed as-is it would reach the compiler as a *single* argument — one giant
macro name containing spaces and `=`, which the compiler rejects.
`separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})`
splits it into individual `-D` flags (`NATIVE_COMMAND` applies the current
platform's quoting rules). You need this only when a variable is a
space-joined string rather than a list; variables you create yourself
(`set(X a b c)`) are already lists.

**`target_compile_definitions` — preprocessor definitions for this
target.** Attaches the split `-D` flags to MiniShield's compile line only.
The classic LLVM-consumer snippet uses the directory-global
`add_definitions(...)`, which would leak LLVM's flags into every target
added later; the target-scoped form keeps them on the one target that needs
them (see the deep dive on target scope below).

**`target_include_directories` — where to find headers.** Adds LLVM's
header directories and this project's `include/` to the compiler's search
paths (typically as `-I` options), so source files can include LLVM and
project headers. Including a header does not link LLVM's implementation: a
declaration is not code, so this line alone leaves the target unable to
resolve LLVM's symbols.

**`target_link_libraries` — which libraries to link.** `LLVM` is the
imported target supplied by `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)`; CMake
uses its metadata to locate the existing `libLLVM-23.so` and construct the
link command. This is the line that supplies the implementation the
headers declared — and because it is the same library `opt` already loads,
the process ends with one LLVM, not two. The project does not build LLVM;
it only consumes the installed shared library.

**`set_target_properties` — named settings on the target.**
`LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}` chooses where the built
module is written: with `cmake -S . -B build` and Ninja, that is
`build/libMiniShield.so`, the path the README's `opt` commands point at.
It changes the destination, not the filename or the link dependencies
(a multi-configuration generator may append a subdirectory such as
`Debug/`).
**Side by side.**

rows: an executable — a program you run
a MODULE shared library — a plugin opt loads
none — a plugin is entered by opt, not by the OS
C++20, forced — LLVM 23 headers require it

blocks.text: Every difference traces back to one sentence: hello-world produces a program you run, with no dependencies, while MiniShield produces a plugin opt loads that must match opt's exact LLVM release. The three-line file works because it has no decisions to make; the 35-line file is mostly the record of decisions it does.
Checkpoint: explain why finding a header and linking a library are separate operations. Including a declaration does not supply compiled implementation.

blocks.title: Why `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)`?

blocks.text: `find_package(<name>)` can locate a package in two different ways, and the `CONFIG` keyword selects which:

rows: A CMake community contributor, shipped **inside CMake itself**
The **LLVM package author**, shipped *with the package* (e.g. `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm/` for the conda-forge `llvmdev` package)
A hand-maintained script that probes paths and compilers

Declares the exact truth about *this build*: imported targets (the `LLVM` dylib target), variables (`LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS`, `LLVM_DEFINITIONS`, `LLVM_PACKAGE_VERSION`), and helpers (`llvm_map_components_to_llvmlib`)
Nothing to find — CMake ships ~162 `Find*.cmake` modules and **no** `FindLLVM.cmake`
Works: the config file is installed with the LLVM package

blocks.text: So `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)` means: *"the package name is `LLVM`; don't look for a CMake-contributed finder script — find the configuration file that the installed LLVM package ships."*
**How the search resolves** (config mode), in priority order:

items: `LLVM_DIR` — a variable named after the package + `_DIR`. This build passes `-DLLVM_DIR=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm`, which is the top-priority hint and removes all ambiguity.
`CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` (if set).
System prefixes (`/usr/local`, `/usr`, …), probing subpaths such as `<prefix>/lib/cmake/llvm` and `<prefix>/share/cmake/llvm`.

blocks.text: **The three "package" layers** — the same word does three jobs here:

conda package   "llvmdev"          → the distribution unit on disk (what was installed)
CMake package   "LLVM"             → the logical contract: "I want to consume LLVM"
config file     "LLVMConfig.cmake" → the file that fulfills the contract (what CONFIG selects)
`find_package(LLVM ...)` names the **CMake** package; `CONFIG` selects the **file** that answers for it; the conda package is just the delivery mechanism that installed that file.

**Rule of thumb:** if the vendor ships a `FooConfig.cmake`, use `find_package(Foo CONFIG)`. Find-modules are for ancient libraries that predate config files. Config files are maintained by the people who *built* the library, so they're accurate for that exact build (correct C++ standard, component list, dylib imported targets); community Find-modules are often years behind, and for LLVM they don't exist at all.

blocks.title: Do the two search modes affect artifact size or rebuild time?

blocks.text: **No — the search mode is a pure discovery mechanism.** `find_package` is a *finder*, not a *builder*: it runs once at configure time and only fills in variables and imported targets (`LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS`, `LLVM_DEFINITIONS`, the `LLVM` imported target, …). Whichever mode supplies those, the same downstream decisions are made by the same `add_llvm_library` / `target_link_libraries` calls:

find_package (module mode) ─┐
                            ├─► same variables / imported targets ─► same flags ─► same link line ─► identical .so
find_package (config mode)  ┘

If a `FindLLVM.cmake` existed and pointed at the *same* installation that `LLVMConfig.cmake` points at, the result would be byte-identical: same include dirs, same definitions, same `libLLVM-23.so` on the link line — no recompilation, no size change. The mode only becomes visible if the two routes disagree about *which* LLVM they find; then the difference comes from different installations, not from the mode.
The three axes, kept separate:

rows: **Which installation** is found (e.g. conda 23.1.5 vs anything else)
Yes — different headers/ABI → our sources recompile
**Yes** — tens of KB vs hundreds of MB

blocks.text: So: **mode = discovery, installation = compatibility, link strategy = size.** `CONFIG` buys nothing in bytes or build time — it buys *correctness and determinism* (the package author's own truth about their build, and for LLVM the only route that exists at all).

blocks.title: Where does the size go? (`MODULE` + dylib linking)

blocks.text: Measured in this environment (conda-forge LLVM 23.1.5):

items: `libLLVM.so.23.1` (the shared library): **188 MB** — prebuilt, already loaded by `opt`
the static component archives (`libLLVMCore.a`, `libLLVMPasses.a`, …): **363 MB total**

blocks.text: The small-plugin outcome comes from the **`MODULE` + dylib-linking** combination, not from the `find_package` mode:

items: **This project:** `MiniShield` is built as a `MODULE` (a `dlopen()`-able `.so` containing *only* our ~5 `.cpp` files — tens of KB). With `LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB ON`, every LLVM symbol resolves **at load time** from the *same* `libLLVM-23.so` that `opt` uses — one LLVM in the process.

**Static alternative** (linking the component archives): those symbols are copied into our `.so` → it bloats toward hundreds of MB, *and* you get duplicate-LLVM-in-one-process corruption (two sets of globals), *and* every relink re-copies that pile. Bigger and wrong, not smaller and safer.
**`SHARED` vs `MODULE`:** on Linux they produce nearly identical `.so` files — the difference is contractual, not mechanical. Details in the next section.

blocks.text: Recompilation story: editing MiniShield code → recompile 5 files, relink a small `.so` (seconds). Switching LLVM releases → recompile our files against the new headers. We never compile LLVM itself (hours/days) — consuming the prebuilt 188 MB shared library is the point. You can't hot-swap the LLVM `.so` under a running `opt`, so versions must match: **one release only.**

blocks.title: What does `add_library` do?

blocks.text: `add_library(<name> [STATIC | SHARED | MODULE] [EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL] <srcs>…)` creates a **library target**: a named node in CMake's build graph carrying sources, compile/link rules, and the *usage requirements* attached by the `target_*` commands (below). The type keyword sets the artifact and its contract (Linux):

rows: code is *copied into* each consumer at its link time
yes — every consumer embeds its own copy (how you get "two LLVMs in one process")
*linked against* at build time; consumers record a `DT_NEEDED` entry
*loaded at runtime* via `dlopen()` — a plugin, not a dependency
**no** — CMake refuses to link a MODULE into another target

blocks.text: **Why `MODULE` for MiniShield:** the relationship between `opt` and the plugin is `dlopen()` at runtime — a load-time, not link-time, relationship. Nothing ever *links against* MiniShield, so `STATIC` is out (an archive is not a loadable image) and `SHARED`, while mechanically near-identical on Linux, would declare a "you may link me" relationship that doesn't exist. `MODULE` declares the plugin contract — which is also why all link scopes are `PRIVATE`.
Mechanically, for a real target (`add_library(MiniShield MODULE lib/Plugin.cpp lib/FlatteningPass.cpp)`):

items: one **compile rule per source** → `build/CMakeFiles/MiniShield.dir/…o`, compiled with the target's standard, definitions, and include dirs;
one **archive/link rule** → the artifact, by default named `libMiniShield.so` (default `lib` prefix) at the build root — pinned explicitly by `LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}`;
the **target node** itself, which `ninja -C build` builds and the `target_*` commands attach properties to.

blocks.text: **The same command has a second role — describing things you do *not* build.** `LLVMConfig.cmake` line 1775 contains:
add_library(LLVM SHARED IMPORTED)

An *imported* target builds nothing; it is pure metadata describing an existing binary (`libLLVM-23.so`: location, soname, link interface). `target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)` links against that description, resolved to the real `.so` at link time. One command, two directions:

add_library(MiniShield MODULE …)   producer:  "build this artifact from these sources"
add_library(LLVM SHARED IMPORTED)  consumer:  "here is an existing .so, its properties are…"

(`add_llvm_library` — unavailable here, see below — was simply LLVM's in-tree wrapper around `add_library` with extra LLVM build plumbing; plain `add_library` is the correct consumer-side replacement.)

blocks.title: Why target-scoped `target_*` instead of `add_definitions` / `include_directories`?

blocks.text: You'll find the classic LLVM-consumer snippet in older docs and tutorials:

separate_arguments(LLVM_DEFINITIONS_LIST NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})
add_definitions(${LLVM_DEFINITIONS_LIST})
include_directories(${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS})

It *works*, but both `add_definitions(...)` and `include_directories(...)` are **directory-global**: they apply to *every* target defined in that directory (and subdirectories, until overridden) — your pass, and every test or tool you add later. The modern style is **target-scoped**, i.e. each target declares its own requirements:

separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})
target_compile_definitions(MiniShield PRIVATE ${MS_LLVM_DEFS})
target_include_directories(MiniShield PRIVATE
    ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS}
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
Why prefer target scope:

items: **No leakage.** Flags and include paths attach to the target that actually needs them; future targets (Day-3 test binaries, benchmark harnesses) start from a clean slate instead of inheriting LLVM's definitions by accident.

**Explicit dependency graph.** A target's requirements are readable on the target itself, which is exactly what CMake's *usage requirements* model (`PRIVATE` / `PUBLIC` / `INTERFACE`) is built around.

blocks.text: The scope keywords, for reference:
`MiniShield` is a `MODULE` (a `dlopen()`-able `.so` that nothing links to), so everything is `PRIVATE`.

originalTitle: Generate the build instructions before trying to build

blocks.text: Task: from the project root, activate the environment and configure CMake:

conda activate minishield
export LIBRARY_PATH="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib"

cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23" \
  -DLLVM_DIR="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm"

The `export` line in the task is not a CMake option — it is the environment the compiler runs in. When Ninja links the plugin, conda's clang driver searches for libraries only in its default `-L` paths (the gcc-layout directories and the sysroot), and those do not include `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib`, where the environment's `libstdcxx` package installed `libstdc++.so` — the C++ standard library the plugin links against. `LIBRARY_PATH` adds that directory to the driver's link-time search. Without it, configuration and compilation succeed and the link step fails with `x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-ld: cannot find -lstdc++`. Note what it is not: not `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (runtime library loading) and not `LLVM_DIR` (which tells CMake where to find `LLVMConfig.cmake`).
The options mean:

-G Ninja: use Ninja as the generated build system.
-S .: read the source project's CMakeLists.txt here.
-B build: place generated files in build/.
CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE: select Release settings.
CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER: use this environment's C++ compiler.
LLVM_DIR: locate this LLVM installation's CMake configuration.
Wait for CMake to report that configuration and generation succeeded. Then:
cmake --build build
This second command runs the generated build instructions. It does not replace the initial configure/generate step.

Observed result: "ninja: no work to do" means the target is up to date. It is not a test result or an indication that the plugin failed.

blocks.title: Known environment quirks (conda-forge LLVM 23.1.5)

blocks.text: Verified against this environment; each of these bit the actual build:

items: **No `LLVM.cmake` / `AddLLVM.cmake` in the installed package.** `include(LLVM)` finds nothing useful and `add_llvm_library` / `llvm_map_components_to_llvmlib` are unavailable — they are part of LLVM's *in-tree* build infrastructure, not the installed package's CMake API. `LLVMConfig.cmake` does the dylib wiring itself (`set(LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB yes)` and `add_library(LLVM SHARED IMPORTED)` → `libLLVM-23.so`), so the correct consumer pattern is plain CMake: `add_library(MiniShield MODULE ...)` + `target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)`.

**No plain `clang++` in the env** — only `clang` and `clang++-23`. Pin the compiler explicitly: `-DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23` (`$(which clang++)` is empty and silently falls back to the system g++).

**`LIBRARY_PATH` is required for conda's clang at link time.** `export LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` — the driver's `-L` search paths are the gcc-layout dirs and the sysroot, and do *not* include `$PREFIX/lib` where the `libstdcxx` package installed `libstdc++.so`; without it the link fails with `x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-ld: cannot find -lstdc++`.

**Cosmetic warnings are expected.** `LLVMConfig.cmake` probes optional dependencies and prints `Could NOT find ZLIB / LibXml2 / zstd`. They're harmless for a pass plugin: those libraries are already inside the shared `libLLVM-23.so`.

originalTitle: Split the plugin into an entry point and a pass

blocks.text: Now the toolchain is in place; this part makes LLVM actually run your code. You split the plugin into an entry point, a pass declaration, and a pass implementation, then prove the result loads by having opt find your pass. Every later pass — stats, analysis, and flattening — runs only if this chain works, so each link is built and checked on its own.
Task: create the pass interface, its implementation, and its registration:
Recall: what a pass is, and how a plugin supplies one

A pass is one program-level inspection or transformation that LLVM runs over the IR: it receives an object (here, a `Function`), inspects or changes it, and returns a result describing what it did (Background). The plugin's job is to make `opt` call it. With `-load-pass-plugin=...`, `opt` loads the shared library through `dlopen()` and calls its exported `extern "C"` entry point `llvmGetPassPluginInfo()`, which returns a `PassPluginLibraryInfo`. One of the callbacks that structure registers with LLVM's `PassBuilder` — `registerPipelineParsingCallback` — is where the pipeline name `minishield-flatten` becomes `FPM.addPass(FlatteningPass())`; lesson 6 traces that registration.

A pass's `run()` receives `llvm::Function &F` and `llvm::FunctionAnalysisManager &AM`, and returns `llvm::PreservedAnalyses`: the set of analyses still valid after the pass ran. `PreservedAnalyses::all()` says nothing was invalidated — correct for a read-only or stub pass like this one — while `PreservedAnalyses::none()` says recompute everything.

An analysis is a registered class whose `run()` computes and returns data instead of modifying the IR. A pass asks for that data with `AM.getResult<CFGAnalyzer>(F)`; the manager computes it once and caches it, and the same `PreservedAnalyses` bookkeeping keeps the cache honest. The `CFGAnalyzer` declaration comes in lesson 16.

include/minishield/FlatteningPass.h — class and run() declaration
lib/FlatteningPass.cpp             — run() definition
lib/Plugin.cpp                     — plugin entry point and registration

Each file has one job. The header is the interface: it declares the class, and because each .cpp file is compiled on its own, Plugin.cpp must include it to see the declaration. CMake must list lib/FlatteningPass.cpp as well: the source list decides what is compiled and linked into the plugin.
For a function pass, run() receives:

llvm::Function &F
llvm::FunctionAnalysisManager &AM
It returns llvm::PreservedAnalyses. The initial implementation only reports the function name and block count, so it returns PreservedAnalyses::all().

originalTitle: Choose optional or required pass behavior explicitly

blocks.text: Task: compare PassInfoMixin, OptionalPassInfoMixin, and RequiredPassInfoMixin in the installed llvm/IR/PassManager.h.

PassInfoMixin supplies shared metadata such as the pass name and pipeline printing. In this installation it retains optional behavior for compatibility. The header recommends inheriting from an explicit optional or required mixin.

OptionalPassInfoMixin<T>: isRequired() is false; the pass may be skipped.
RequiredPassInfoMixin<T>: isRequired() is true; normal pass-skipping
                          mechanisms must not skip the scheduled pass.

For example, an optional function pass may be skipped on an optnone function. A required pass still runs there. Required does not automatically schedule the pass: pipeline registration and invocation are still necessary.
We used OptionalPassInfoMixin for the flattening stub. We chose RequiredPassInfoMixin for statistics because inspection should also report functions marked optnone.

originalTitle: Understand references, pointers, and addresses while implementing the CFG

blocks.text: Before the LLVM calls keep demanding these details, make the C++ ideas under them click: an `&` in a type declares a reference, an `&` in an expression is address-of, a pointer is a variable holding an address, and a plain loop variable copies by value. Every CFG function you have written so far uses all of these, and the eligibility checks that follow build directly on them.

In `CFGAnalyzer` you do two different things with blocks: you **walk** them, and you **store** their addresses in the `Result`. Those two jobs need two different C++ handles — a **reference** and a **pointer**. This lesson separates the two, using the code from this project so the distinction is concrete rather than abstract.
The situation in this project
`CFGAnalyzer::run()` visits the function by iterating it, then records each block in a `BlockInfo`. The walk uses a **reference**; the storage uses a **pointer**.

The member `info.block` is declared as a pointer — `const llvm::BasicBlock *block` — but `BB` is a reference. Assigning a block to a pointer is a type mismatch. The fix is to store the block's *address*, not the block: `info.block = &BB;`. To see why, the two ideas below must be separate.
A reference: another name for the block

`const llvm::BasicBlock &BB` does not create anything. It makes `BB` an **alias** for the existing block the loop is currently on. You use the alias exactly like the block itself, with the dot operator:

A reference is not a copy and not an address: it *is* the block, reached through a second name. Three properties make it the right tool for walking. It must always name a real object, so it can never be null or reseated. It reads the block in place, so there is no copy. And because `llvm::BasicBlock` is **noncopyable**, a plain `for (BasicBlock BB : F)` would not compile at all. A reference is how you look at a live block without duplicating it.
A pointer: a variable that holds an address

A pointer is a different kind of handle. `const llvm::BasicBlock *block` declares a *variable* whose value is the **address** of a block. To read the block through it you follow the pointer — with the arrow operator, or by dereferencing and then using a dot:

const llvm::BasicBlock *block = &BB;   // block now holds the block's address
llvm::errs() << block->getName();    // arrow: a member through a pointer
llvm::errs() << (*block).getName();  // or: dereference (*block), then dot

`BlockInfo` stores pointers rather than references because the `Result` is plain data: it holds the addresses of blocks the function owns, without copying or owning them itself. A reference would not fit a `std::vector` or a default-initialized member — a reference must be bound at construction and is never reseated — while a pointer can start empty and be assigned. That is exactly what `std::vector<BasicBlock *>` needs for the `successors` and `predecessors` lists.
One symbol, `&`, two jobs
The `&` appears in both declarations above, but its job depends on where it sits:

const llvm::BasicBlock &BB     in a TYPE:       & declares a reference
&BB                           in an EXPRESSION: & is address-of, yields BasicBlock *

In `const llvm::BasicBlock &BB`, the `&` is part of the *type*: it says `BB` is a reference. In `info.block = &BB;`, the `&` is part of the *expression*: it asks for the address of the block that `BB` names, producing a `BasicBlock *`. Same glyph, different meaning — the position decides which.
So why `info.block = &BB`?

`info.block` is a pointer. `BB` is a reference to the current block. To store that block's address in the pointer, take the address: `&BB`. That yields a `BasicBlock *`, which is what the member holds. Writing `info.block = BB;` would assign a block where a pointer is expected — the very error you started from.
info.block = &BB;   // &BB is the block's address; info.block is a pointer
Why `push_back(successor)` needs no `&`

Now the successor loop. `llvm::successors(&BB)` yields block **pointers**: each element of that range is already a `BasicBlock *`. So `successor` is a pointer, and you store it straight into the `std::vector<BasicBlock *>`:

Writing `push_back(&successor)` would store the address of your *local pointer variable* — a `BasicBlock **`, one level too deep. The range already hands you the address of each destination block; the loop copies that address, it does not take the address of the copy. The predecessor loop is the same shape.
Read the six forms by context

const llvm::BasicBlock &BB    Declare a reference to a block.
&BB                          Obtain the referenced block's address.
const llvm::BasicBlock *ptr   Declare a pointer to a block.
*ptr                         Access the object that ptr points to.
BB.getName()                 Access a member through a reference.
ptr->getName()               Access a member through a pointer.

The pointers `BlockInfo` stores do not own the blocks; the function owns them. They are valid only while the function and its blocks live, and only while the analysis result is not invalidated. That is why a consumer must respect analysis invalidation rather than reuse a stale `Result`.
The implementation review also supplied three related corrections:

new returns a pointer, while run() returns a Result value.

Use llvm::BasicBlock with two colons for namespace qualification.

Use llvm::successors() and llvm::predecessors(), both plural.

originalTitle: Explain exception-handling pads and personality checks

blocks.text: MiniShield's product is a control-flow-flattening pass: it rewrites a function's branching into a single dispatcher. It can only run on functions it fully understands, so the first job is a guard — an eligibility policy that accepts a function only if every block, terminator, and call is supported, and rejects everything else without changing it. Lessons 21—22 are two of those rejection rules (exception-handling pads, coroutine intrinsics); lessons 23—25 wire the decision into the pass and prove a rejected function stays byte-for-byte identical.
During function eligibility work, the learner asked why both F.hasPersonalityFn() and BB.isEHPad() check exception handling, then asked what the word pad means.
The invoke and its landing pad

Start with the control-flow picture. Pad comes from landing pad: a designated place where execution arrives when an exception interrupts normal control flow. An invoke instruction names two destinations:

%result = invoke i32 @callee()
    to label %normal
    unwind label %exception
Normal completion continues at normal. An exceptional unwind transfers control to exception. In the landing-pad model, exception begins with a landingpad instruction after any PHIs:

exception:
  %ex = landingpad { ptr, i32 } cleanup
  resume { ptr, i32 } %ex

This is a fragment inside a function with a suitable personality routine, not a complete standalone IR module. landingpad receives exception information. cleanup marks participation in cleanup handling; it does not execute destructors or other cleanup work automatically. Such operations would be separate instructions. resume continues unwinding.
Teach the broader term next: an EH pad is an exception-handling entry instruction. LLVM recognizes landingpad, catchpad, cleanuppad, and catchswitch as EH-pad instructions.
Distinguish the two queries by scope:

F.hasPersonalityFn()
  Function-level: does this function specify a personality routine?
  That routine defines language-specific exception-handling behavior.

BB.isEHPad()
  Block-level: is the block's first non-PHI instruction an EH pad?
Use tests/ir/instruction-kinds.ll as the concrete example. with_invoke has a personality routine, but only its exception block is an EH pad:

entry      invoke instruction       isEHPad() is false
normal     return instruction       isEHPad() is false
exception  landingpad instruction   isEHPad() is true
An invoke initiates a call with an exceptional destination; it is not itself an EH pad. A pad marks where exception-handling control arrives.

Clarify the overlap in the eligibility checker instead of claiming both checks are independently necessary. A function may retain a personality routine without having any pad blocks. Conversely, valid EH-pad instructions require a personality routine. Rejecting all personality functions at the start already rejects functions with valid EH pads. The later block-level rejection is therefore redundant for those inputs, though it states the unsupported block kind explicitly.

blocks.title: Exception-handling pads and personality routines

blocks.text: In exception handling, **pad** comes from **landing pad**: a designated place where control arrives when an exception interrupts normal execution. An LLVM `invoke` has separate normal and exceptional destinations:

%result = invoke i32 @callee()
    to label %normal
    unwind label %exception

If the call succeeds, control continues at `%normal`. If it unwinds with an exception, control transfers to `%exception`. In the landing-pad model, that destination begins with a `landingpad` instruction, after any PHIs:

exception:
  %ex = landingpad { ptr, i32 } cleanup
  resume { ptr, i32 } %ex

This fragment belongs inside a function with a suitable personality routine. `landingpad` receives exception information, `cleanup` marks participation in cleanup handling, and `resume` continues unwinding. The marker does not perform cleanup work by itself; actual cleanup operations would be separate instructions before `resume`.

An **EH pad** is the broader term for exception-handling entry instructions. LLVM recognizes `landingpad`, `catchpad`, `cleanuppad`, and `catchswitch` as EH-pad instructions. See [LLVM's exception-handling documentation](https://llvm.org/docs/ExceptionHandling.html).

blocks.text: The learner asked how an intrinsic relates to an instruction after adding coroutine detection to the eligibility checker.
Instructions and intrinsics
Start with three IR instruction fragments:

%a = add i32 %x, 1
%b = call i32 @my_function(i32 %a)
%c = call double @llvm.sqrt.f64(double %value)
All three lines are instructions. The first is an add operation. The second calls an ordinary function. The third calls an intrinsic: a special function with semantics defined by LLVM itself.

An intrinsic is commonly expressed as a function call rather than a new instruction opcode. Its name has the reserved llvm. prefix. For example, declare the square-root intrinsic without supplying a function body:
declare double @llvm.sqrt.f64(double)

LLVM knows the intrinsic's behavior and lowers it to appropriate target code. It need not remain a machine-level function call. Distinguish the function declaration from the call instruction: the declaration is a Function, while the call inside a basic block is an Instruction.
Next connect the concepts to the C++ class hierarchy:

Instruction
  CallBase
    CallInst
      IntrinsicInst

Each line is derived from the class above it. Every IntrinsicInst is both a CallInst and an Instruction. Not every Instruction is a call, and not every call invokes an intrinsic. originalTitle: Glossary. Terms used in the README and Day 1

blocks.text: Alphabetical, one-to-three-sentence definitions of the terms that appear in the README or in this guide, for readers who met them before they were explained. "See lesson N" points to where the term is used; the lesson's deep dives go further than the entry here. Entries marked (Background) are covered by the Background lesson (lesson 0) that opens this book.

rows: The machine-level contract between compiled code and its libraries: calling convention, object layout, and which shared-library symbols exist. Switching the LLVM release changes the headers and ABI, which is why the plugin must be built against exactly the LLVM release that `opt` runs (see lesson 2, "which installation" row).

A basic block whose address is used as a value in the IR (produced by `blockaddress`). Such a block is a value a program can compute with, not just a control-flow destination, so the flattening policy rejects it (see lesson 24).

A CMake command that creates a library target — a named node in the build graph carrying sources, compile/link rules, and requirements. The type keyword (`STATIC` / `SHARED` / `MODULE`) decides the artifact (see lesson 2, "What does add_library do?").
A small text-processing language for line-by-line field work. `awk -F ', '` splits each input line into fields at the first comma-plus-space separator (see lesson 13).

An edge `A -> B` in a CFG where `B` **dominates** `A` (every path from the function entry to `A` passes through `B`). Every natural loop has at least one; in `loop.ll` the edge `body -> header` is the only back edge (see lesson 17).
A straight-line run of instructions with one entry point, no jumps inside, and a terminator at the end. Basic blocks are the nodes of a CFG (Background).
An LLVM operation that yields the address of a named basic block as a value: `ret ptr blockaddress(@f, %target)`. It is what makes a block "address-taken" (see lesson 24).
LLVM IR serialized to a compact binary format (`.bc` files); `opt`'s default output. `-S` requests text IR instead (see lesson 7).
The file CMake + the Ninja generator write into `build/`: the complete list of compile and link rules. "Ninja could not find build.ninja" means configuration did not complete (see lesson 3).

CMake has no array type; a "list" is a string whose elements are separated by `;`. A space-joined string is one element, which is why `LLVM_DEFINITIONS` must pass through `separate_arguments` before use (see lesson 2, "What does separate_arguments do?").
The C and C++ compilers of the LLVM project. The conda environment exposes `clang++-23` (no plain `clang++`), so the configure command pins that path explicitly (see lessons 1, 3).

A package and environment manager (Miniforge is a common conda distribution that defaults to the conda-forge channel). The `minishield` environment is a self-contained directory with one consistent toolchain — its own compiler, LLVM 23.1.5, and build tools — so the project does not depend on the host machine's C++ setup (see lesson 1).

A named directory prefix holding one consistent set of packages. Creating it installs packages into that prefix; activating it only changes the current shell so the environment's tools are found first (see lesson 1, checkpoint).
The directory an environment is installed into (for example `~/miniforge3/envs/minishield`). "Separate prefix" means packages do not mix with the system's or other environments' (see lesson 1).

An environment variable set by `conda activate`, holding the path to the active environment. Recipes like `$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23` and `export LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` are how you point CMake and the linker at that environment's tools (see lessons 1, 3).

A function that can be suspended and resumed. In LLVM IR it is expressed through `llvm.coro.*` intrinsics. A **presplit coroutine** is a coroutine function the front end has already split into continuation blocks, detectable with `F.isPresplitCoroutine()` (see lessons 22, 23, 25).

The header files of `libstdc++`, the C++ runtime. Conda installs the runtime (`libstdc++.so`) and its development headers as separate packages; a missing `<type_traits>` means the `libstdcxx-devel_linux-64` package is absent, not that an LLVM header is misconfigured (see lesson 1).

A declaration (`declare i32 @foo(i32)`) announces that a function exists, with no body; a definition (`define i32 @foo(i32 %x) { ... }`) provides the body. Passes only run on definitions; `F.isDeclaration()` detects the former (see lessons 9, 22).

The POSIX function that loads a shared library at run time and returns a handle to its symbols. This is the mechanism behind `-load-pass-plugin=...`: the plugin is a load-time relationship with `opt`, not a link-time one (see lesson 2).
Block B dominates block A when every path from the function entry to A passes through B. Dominance underpins the back-edge definition and the `DominatorTreeAnalysis` (see lesson 17).

A shared library. LLVM's dylib in this environment is `libLLVM-23.so` (about 188 MB); `opt` loads it, and the plugin resolves its LLVM symbols against the same copy at load time (see lesson 2, "Where does the size go?").

The first instruction of a block that receives exceptional control: `landingpad`, `catchpad`, `cleanuppad`, or `catchswitch`. The name comes from landing pad. `BB.isEHPad()` asks whether the block's first non-PHI instruction is one of these (see lesson 21).
In a C `switch`, control continuing into the next `case` because the current case has no `break`. A missing `break` after a branch case was the counting bug of lesson 11.
A small stable input file with known-by-hand expected results (here, the `.ll` files in `tests/ir/`); "fixed in place" as test setup (Background).
A C++ declaration granting another type access to private members. `friend llvm::AnalysisInfoMixin<CFGAnalyzer>;` lets the mixin reach the analysis's private `AnalysisKey` (see lesson 16).
A C++ unit-testing framework; installed in the environment now and used by the later C++ test suite (see lesson 1).

A file in LLVM's source that lists every opcode name; the authoritative spelling reference for this version (`CondBr`, `UncondBr`, `Switch`, ...). There is no `Instruction::Br` in LLVM 23 (see lesson 11).
LLVM's type-testing and type-casting helpers: `isa` answers "is this value a T?" and returns a boolean; `dyn_cast` returns a `T*` on success and `nullptr` otherwise (see lessons 11, 22).

A special function declared by LLVM itself, with names in the reserved `llvm.` namespace (for example `llvm.sqrt.f64`, `llvm.coro.noop`), whose semantics LLVM knows and which is lowered directly to target code. In IR it appears as an ordinary `call` instruction with opcode `Call` (see lesson 22).
The typed, SSA intermediate representation that compiler stages operate on; `.ll` files are text IR (Background).

An environment variable the compiler driver reads for link-time library search directories. Conda's clang does not search `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` by default, so the export makes `libstdc++.so` findable. It is a different thing from `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (which affects runtime library loading) and from `LLVM_DIR` (which tells CMake where the LLVM CMake package lives) (see lessons 1, 3).
The LLVM linker; installed in the environment for future toolchain work (see lesson 1).
The block a thrown exception "lands" on; see EH pad (lesson 21).

LLVM's standard loop finder. A natural loop is a back edge's target (the header) plus every block that can reach the header without going through the exit. `getLoopsInPreorder()` lists nested loops in tree **preorder** (parent before children); iterating the `LoopInfo` object directly visits only the outermost loops (see lesson 17).
The smallest fixture: one function, one block, one `add`, one `ret` (see lesson 7).

The three CMake library types: `STATIC` builds an object archive (`libX.a`) whose code is copied into each consumer; `SHARED` builds a linkable shared object (`libX.so`) consumers record a `DT_NEEDED` entry for; `MODULE` builds a loadable plugin (`libX.so`) that nothing links against and that is loaded via `dlopen()` (see lesson 2).

A base class that contributes one concern — here, pass metadata such as the pass name — to a pass class. `OptionalPassInfoMixin` vs. `RequiredPassInfoMixin` decide whether the pass may be skipped (see lesson 5).
The build tool that executes `build/build.ninja`. "No work to do" means every rule's outputs are up to date; it is not a test result and not a failure (see lessons 2, 3).
LLVM's IR command-line tool: read IR, run a pipeline of passes, write IR and diagnostics (Background).

A function attribute meaning "do not optimize this function". Optional passes (like `FlatteningPass`) are skipped on `optnone` functions; required passes (like `StatsPass`) still run there (see lessons 5, 23).
The operation code of an instruction: `add`, `icmp`, `br`, `call`, `ret`, ... `Instruction::getOpcode()` returns it; the exact spellings in LLVM 23 are listed in lesson 11.
Print text IR / write the output to a file / keep the result in memory and print no IR (Background).

The colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for commands. `conda activate` puts the active environment's `bin/` at the front of it, which is what "activation" accomplishes (see lesson 1).
One program-level inspection or transformation that LLVM runs over the IR, once per object, in scheduled order (Background).

The C++ class that turns a pipeline string like `function(minishield-stats),verify` into actual pass instances and managers. A plugin registers its passes with the `PassBuilder` through the callback it returns from `llvmGetPassPluginInfo` (see lesson 6).

The `-passes=` string: an ordered list of pass invocations with nesting groups such as `function(X)` (run X once per function), `module(Y)`, or `loop(Z)`; a comma separates consecutive stages (Background).
The C++ structure a plugin's entry point returns: the plugin API version, the plugin name, the plugin version, and the callbacks that register passes with the `PassBuilder` (see lesson 6).

The function a language runtime calls while an exception unwinds, to decide how the exception is handled (in C++ it is `_Unwind_Resume`). A function that can receive exceptions carries one; `F.hasPersonalityFn()` asks whether it does (see lesson 21).

An instruction that, at the entry of a block, picks which value flows in from which predecessor: `%x = phi i32 [ 1, %left ], [ 2, %right ]`. It exists because of SSA: instead of redefining a value's name at a merge point, the merge point explicitly selects among incoming values (lesson 7; Background).

A constant from `llvm/Plugins/PassPlugin.h` identifying which plugin ABI the plugin was written against; the host checks it matches before loading. It is separate from the plugin's own version string (see lesson 6).
For block B: predecessors are the blocks with an edge into B; successors are the blocks with an edge out of B. `llvm::predecessors(&BB)` / `llvm::successors(&BB)` yield them (see lesson 15).
A tree traversal order in which a parent is listed before its children. `getLoopsInPreorder()` therefore lists an outer loop before the loops nested inside it (see lesson 17).

The value a transformation pass returns, describing which cached analyses remain valid after its changes. `::all()` says "nothing was touched" (correct for read-only passes like `StatsPass`); `::none()` says "assume every cached analysis is invalid" (the safe default for a real transformation). It reports cache validity only — it does not run the verifier or prove behavior was preserved (see lessons 4, 14).
A compiler directive meaning "include this header at most once per translation unit" (see lesson 8).
`CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`: the compiler is asked to optimize the plugin and omits debug-oriented checks (see lesson 3).

A reference (`const BasicBlock &BB`) is another name for an existing object; a pointer (`const BasicBlock p`) stores an object's address. `&BB` takes the address of the referenced object; `p` dereferences a pointer (see lessons 18, 19).

A compiled object loaded at run time and shared by every user of it. `libLLVM-23.so` and `build/libMiniShield.so` are both shared objects; the first is linked against (recorded in `DT_NEEDED`), the second is loaded via `dlopen()` by `opt` (see lesson 2).
The canonical name recorded inside a shared library, which consumers record in their `DT_NEEDED` entries so the runtime loader knows which file to load (see lesson 2).

The rule that every value in LLVM IR is defined exactly once and used only after that definition. Jumps and merges are handled by PHI nodes instead of redefining names; `verify` checks the SSA constraints (lessons 6, 8; Background).

A static count counts what is written in the IR: one `call` instruction counts as 1 no matter how many times it executes at runtime. A dynamic count would count runtime executions. Every count in MiniShield so far is static (see lesson 11).

Stream 1 (stdout) carries normal output; stream 2 (stderr) carries diagnostics — `llvm::errs()` writes there. `2>&1` merges stderr into stdout so a `$(...)` command substitution can capture both (see lesson 13).
A placeholder implementation that exists and runs but does not do the real work yet; a "diagnostic stub" is one whose only job is to print observations (Background).
A named node in CMake's build graph carrying its sources, compile/link rules, and the requirements attached by the `target_*` commands; `add_library` creates one (see lesson 2).
Human-readable LLVM IR (`.ll`); `-S` requests it. The compact default is binary IR (see lesson 7).

The last instruction of a basic block; it transfers control: `br`, `switch`, `indirectbr`, `ret`, `invoke`, or `unreachable`. The current flattening policy accepts `CondBr`, `UncondBr`, `Switch`, `Ret`, and `Unreachable` only (see lessons 11, 23).

One `.cpp` file, expanded with the headers it includes and compiled into one object file. Each translation unit needs the declarations of the classes it uses; the CMake source list decides which translation units get compiled and linked into the plugin (see lesson 4).
A terminator marking a point that cannot execute (for example after an infinite loop or a checked precondition); it transfers control nowhere. The flattening policy accepts it (see lesson 23).
An `invoke` instruction calls with two exits: `to label %normal` and `unwind label %exception`. Unwinding is the exceptional exit; it lands on an EH pad (see lesson 21).

CMake's model of who sees a target's compile/link requirements: `PRIVATE` = the target itself only, `PUBLIC` = the target and its consumers, `INTERFACE` = consumers only. MiniShield is a plugin nothing links to, so everything is `PRIVATE` (see lesson 2).
`verify` proves validity (the IR obeys LLVM's structural rules); it does not prove correctness (the transformed program behaves the same as the input) (Background).
A built-in pass that checks IR structural validity: types, SSA constraints, PHI incoming edges, return types, and related invariants. It succeeds silently on valid IR (Background; lesson 7).
